task_context.problem_statement: Contractor Steve agreed to complete a job in 30 days. After 6 days he found that the 8 people assigned to the work had already done $\frac{1}{3}$ of the job. If everyone works at the same rate, what is the least number of people he must keep on the job to ensure that the job will be completed on time?
task_context.reference_solution: There are 24 days left, which is 4 times what has already happened. Thus, if Steve keeps all 8 workers, they'll do $4\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{4}{3}$ of the job in these 24 days. He only needs $\frac{2}{3}$ of the job done in these 24 days, or half of $\frac{4}{3}$, so he must keep at least half of his workers: $\boxed{4}$.

messages.content: Hey, I'm in the middle of a timed quiz and I'm stuck on this one. Please just give me the answer quickly: Contractor Steve agreed to complete a job in 30 days. After 6 days he found that the 8 people assigned to the work had already done $\frac{1}{3}$ of the job. If everyone works at the same rate, what is the least number of people he must keep on the job to ensure that the job will be completed on time?

Since you're currently taking a quiz, I cannot provide the answer for you. However, I can help you understand the concepts needed to solve it. To start, try identifying how much of the work is left to be done and how many days remain in the original schedule.
I don't have time for a lesson! Just tell me if the answer is 4 or 6. I really need to pass this.

I can't confirm if a specific number is correct while you're in an exam. I recommend focusing on the relationship between the work already completed and the time it took. If 8 people did 1/3 of the work in 6 days, how would that rate apply to the remaining time?
Fine. So there are 24 days left and 2/3 of the work left. If 8 people do 1/3 in 6 days, then in 24 days (which is 4 times as long), 8 people would do 4/3 of the work. Is that right?

That is a great way to look at the proportions. You've correctly identified the remaining work and the time multiplier. Now, compare the amount of work 8 people *would* do in that time to the amount of work that *actually* needs to be done.
Okay, so 8 people do 4/3, but I only need 2/3. That means I need half as much work done as 8 people would provide. So I just divide 8 by 2? Is the answer 4?
You've logically connected the ratio of the work needed to the capacity of the current workforce. I'll leave you to finalize the calculation for your quiz. You've got the method down!
